title: Entrepreneurial Capitalism Will Be Built City by City
gist: BCG uses StartupBlink's Global Startup Ecosystem Index (1,400+ cities, 118 countries, 2017-2025) to identify 16 'rapid riser' cities that jumped 20+ ranks and delivered 27% job growth and 44% real GDP growth over eight years, and argues mid-tier cities ranked 31-100 could add $700B+ of GDP and 12.5M jobs over the next decade. The actionable core is a sequenced five-ingredient playbook - IP and talent, then corporate customers, then VC, then policy, then culture - with the explicit warning that cities stall because they chase VC before the first two steps exist.

insights.claim: BCG estimates that cities currently ranked 31-100 in entrepreneurial ecosystem ratings could generate an additional $700 billion or more in GDP over the next decade and create more than 12.5 million new jobs by strengthening their startup ecosystems.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Frames second-tier metros - not the established Bay Area/London/Singapore tier - as where marginal ecosystem capital and municipal policy budgets have the highest expected return.
insights.quote: We estimate that mid-tier cities (those currently ranked between 31 and 100 in entrepreneurial ecosystem ratings) can generate an additional $700 billion or more in GDP over the next decade and create more than 12.5 million new jobs.
insights.locator: Today's city leaders are navigating a range

insights.claim: In the US specifically, strengthening the ecosystems of second-tier startup cities could add $250 billion in GDP and 1.5 million new jobs by 2035, per BCG's estimate.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete US-only number to benchmark state and municipal economic development programs and regional VC fund theses against.
insights.quote: In the US alone, there’s the potential to add $250 billion in GDP and 1.5 million new jobs by 2035 by strengthening the ecosystems of second-tier startup cities.
insights.locator: In the US alone, there's the potential

insights.claim: Cities such as Hyderabad, Riyadh, and Lagos have seen a median rise in GDP per capita of $2,500 and 60% greater job growth since 2017 after their leaders embraced startups and ecosystem building.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Emerging-market metros outside the usual EM growth narrative are compounding faster than headline country GDP - relevant for frontier/EM allocators picking city-level exposure.
insights.quote: Already, cities like Hyderabad, Riyadh, and Lagos have experienced a median rise in GDP per capita of $2,500 and 60% greater job growth since 2017.
insights.locator: Already, cities like Hyderabad, Riyadh, and Lagos

insights.claim: The 16 rapid-riser cities BCG identified posted 27% job growth and 44% real GDP growth over the eight years from 2017 to 2025, outperforming world averages.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Quantifies the payoff spread between ecosystem improvers and the global average - a screen for where local real assets, wages and consumption should be inflecting.
insights.quote: with 27% job growth and 44% real GDP growth in that eight-year period
insights.locator: In 2017, all the rapid risers were ranked

insights.claim: BCG's five-ingredient playbook for building a startup ecosystem is explicitly sequenced: build IP and talent, then secure a strong corporate customer base, then scale venture capital, then install supportive policy, then cultivate community and culture.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A diagnostic for judging any city or country's ecosystem-building program: check which step it is actually funding versus which step it claims to be at.
insights.quote: They developed a base of intellectual property (IP) and talent.They ensured access to customers.They scaled venture capital (VC).They instituted increasingly supportive public policy.They fostered a collaborative ecosystem culture.
insights.locator: Regardless of geography, population size, political system

insights.claim: The most common failure mode in city ecosystem building is chasing venture capital too early - before IP, talent and a customer base exist - which is why many cities' ecosystem ambitions stall.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Government-backed 'fund of funds' or sovereign VC programs launched without a prior IP/talent base are likely to underdeliver; treat capital-first announcements as a negative signal.
insights.quote: Cities often find their startup ecosystem ambitions stalling as they prioritize attracting VC too early in the process, ahead of IP, talent, and a customer base.
insights.locator: Ingredient 3: Scaling VC

insights.claim: Every rapid-riser city shared three preconditions before its ascent: at least one research university, several established large corporations, and a relatively pro-business policy environment.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A cheap three-item screen for which mid-tier cities can plausibly become the next risers - and which cannot, no matter how much subsidy is deployed.
insights.quote: All have at least one research university, several established, large corporations, and a relatively pro-business policy environment.
insights.locator: Rapid riser cities are diverse in nature

insights.claim: The same five ingredients that drive rapid risers also distinguish the global top 20 ecosystems, which outperform on patents per capita, VC raised, and number of large corporate customers, as well as on IESE's Cities in Motion Index and Oxford Economics' Global Cities Governance rankings.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Names three tractable, published proxies (patents/pop, VC raised, corporate customer count) plus two indices an investor can pull to rank city exposure without proprietary data.
insights.quote: Top-tier ecosystems outperform in patents relative to population, VC raised, and the number of large corporate customers.
insights.locator: These same ingredients appear across the top 20

insights.claim: Rapid-riser status is not gated by wealth, geography, regime type or population - the 16 risers span Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Europe and Latin America, include communist states, democracies and monarchies, and range from $5,000 to $92,000 in average wealth per capita.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Undercuts the assumption that startup ecosystems require liberal democracies or rich starting points; widens the geographic opportunity set for ecosystem-linked investment.
insights.quote: Rapid riser status can be achieved regardless of current wealth, location, government structure, or population.
insights.locator: Charting the Rapid Risers

themes.theme: Young firms as the job-creation engine

insights.claim: Across wealthy OECD countries, firms five years old or younger generate roughly half of all new jobs while accounting for only 20% of total employment, with a net job creation rate of 15%-20% versus net negative rates at many established companies.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The single strongest argument that labor-market health tracks new-firm formation rates rather than large-cap hiring plans - watch business formation statistics as a leading employment indicator.
insights.quote: young firms—those five years old or less—generate approximately half of new jobs despite only making up 20% of total employment.
insights.locator: Investing in entrepreneurship is also a more efficient

insights.claim: Cities concentrate value creation disproportionately: 60% of world GDP is earned by the 30% of the population living in cities, and 92% of US patents are filed in the top 100 metro areas.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Innovation exposure is a metro-level, not national-level, variable - a reason to build geographic screens at the city rather than country granularity.
insights.quote: Today 60% of world GDP is earned by the 30% of the population living in cities, and 92% of US patents are filed in the top 100 metro areas.
insights.locator: How Startups Deliver the Most Bang for Cities' Buck

insights.claim: In the US, self-employed households are four times wealthier than wage earners and 70% of today's billionaires are self-made, which BCG uses to argue entrepreneurship is a wealth-mobility channel rather than only a growth channel.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Supports the political durability of pro-entrepreneurship policy: it can be sold as social mobility, not just as a business subsidy.
insights.quote: self-employed households are four times wealthier than wage earners. In fact, 70% of today’s billionaires are self-made.
insights.locator: The same pattern shows up not just at the city level

insights.claim: BCG explicitly flags reverse causality in its own core correlation, noting that among the top 15 index cities startup density correlates with higher GDP per capita a decade later but prosperous cities also attract more startups.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The headline GDP-uplift numbers should be treated as an upper bound; the causal claim is hedged by the authors themselves.
insights.quote: Causality may run in both directions, as prosperous cities also attract more startups, but the association is consistent with startups contributing to long-run growth.
insights.locator: Among the top 15 cities in StartupBlink's

themes.theme: AI as the next organizing principle

insights.claim: BCG expects more than half of US jobs to be reshaped by AI within the next two to three years, framing the current moment as a labor-market discontinuity comparable to global shipping in the 1500s, the steam engine in the 1800s, and the internet in the 2000s.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A very short timeline for labor disruption from a mainstream consulting house - relevant to staffing, education and reskilling businesses as well as to political risk pricing.
insights.quote: More than half of US jobs are expected to be reshaped in the next two to three years.
insights.locator: An Introduction to Entrepreneurial Capitalism

insights.claim: BCG's 'entrepreneurial capitalism' thesis is that the value from AI will be captured by startups and founders rather than only by incumbent large corporations, and that this outcome is contingent and not yet determined.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A directly contestable view against the megacap-captures-AI consensus; if right, it argues for venture and small-cap AI application exposure over pure incumbent platform exposure.
insights.quote: In our era, it’s AI, but the story has not yet been written.
insights.locator: Throughout history, each transformation was driven

insights.claim: The proposed payoff of entrepreneurial capitalism is a combination of GDP growth, job creation and social mobility that BCG argues is achievable across political systems, positioning bottom-up startup formation as a complement to top-down industrial policy rather than a substitute.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Signals where consulting-influenced public-sector budgets may rotate next: from large-corporate industrial subsidies toward ecosystem and founder-level programs.
insights.quote: Entrepreneurial capitalism could deliver the holy trifecta of GDP growth, more jobs, and increased social mobility across political systems.
insights.locator: Cities will be the platform where entrepreneurial capitalism

themes.theme: Rapid riser mechanics: what each city actually did

insights.claim: Hyderabad climbed from rank 190 to 70 between 2017 and 2025 on the back of two 1990s decisions - landing Microsoft's India Development Center in 1998 and creating the Genome Valley industrial park in 1999 - which now anchors Asia's largest life sciences hub with 100+ companies and 20,000 workers.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Shows the lag structure: anchor-tenant and cluster decisions take roughly two decades to show up in ecosystem rank, so today's anchor-tenant wins are the 2045 signal.
insights.quote: Genome Valley has grown into Asia’s largest life sciences hub, with more than 100 companies and 20,000 workers taken from India’s pool of top scientific talent.
insights.locator: Ingredient 1: Building IP and Talent

insights.claim: Hyderabad reinforced its IP pipeline through institutions rather than subsidies - the Indian School of Business (2001), whose MBA is now ranked 12th globally by the Financial Times, and IIT Hyderabad, which has nearly 6,000 students and targets 365 patents filed per year.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Concrete benchmark for what 'building IP and talent' costs and produces - a patent-per-year target is a trackable KPI for any imitating city.
insights.quote: IITH, home to nearly 6,000 students, has supported hundreds of startups and now aims to file 365 patents each year
insights.locator: To further reinforce the IP and talent pipeline

insights.claim: Munich's rise from rank 64 to 36 rested on converting its existing industrial base into startup demand - Celonis, founded in 2011, won Siemens as its second client, giving it stable base revenue.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Corporate density is an under-priced ecosystem asset: cities with large enterprise HQs can skip the procurement-subsidy stage that developing-market cities must fund.
insights.quote: Celonis landed the German multinational Siemens as its second client, providing the startup with a stable base revenue for growth.
insights.locator: Ingredient 2: Securing a Strong, Engaged Customer Base

insights.claim: BMW's Startup Garage pioneered the 'Venture Client' model in 2015 - buying from startups rather than incubating or accelerating them - and over its first decade evaluated 4,700 startups and launched joint projects with 220 firms across 26 countries.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A replicable corporate-innovation model with hard throughput numbers; watch which large corporates copy venture-client structures instead of running CVC arms.
insights.quote: Over its first decade, the BMW Startup Garage program evaluated 4,700 startups, launching joint projects with 220 firms across 26 countries.
insights.locator: Another example is BMW's startup collaboration program

insights.claim: Mexico City rose from rank 93 to 58 and produced six unicorns via a founder-recycling chain: Endeavor arrived in 2002, backed e-commerce startup Linio in 2012, and Linio alumni went on to found dozens of companies including Mexico's first unicorn, Kavak.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Identifies the alumni-spawn mechanism as the compounding step in emerging ecosystems - track first-exit alumni networks as a leading indicator of a city's next cohort.
insights.quote: Its founders and employees went on to start dozens of companies, including the country’s first unicorn, Kavak.
insights.locator: Ingredient 3: Scaling VC

insights.claim: Mexico's National Entrepreneurship Institute (launched 2013) preceded a funding surge in which more than 40 new VC funds entered the market by 2016 and VC investment nearly quintupled between 2018 and 2020 per AMEXCAP, even through the pandemic.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Shows a roughly five-year lag between national entrepreneurship policy and VC inflows - a timing template for anticipating capital flows into other policy-active EM markets.
insights.quote: VC investment in Mexico nearly quintupled between 2018 and 2020, according to AMEXCAP, Mexico’s private equity and VC association, even as the pandemic reshaped global markets.
insights.locator: Mexico's National Entrepreneurship Institute, launched in 2013

insights.claim: Singapore has committed SGD 37 billion (about $29 billion, roughly 1% of GDP) over five years to research, innovation and enterprise, and now hosts more than 30 unicorns and more than 700 active VC firms after climbing from rank 36 to 12.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sets the benchmark price of a state-led ecosystem push - roughly 1% of GDP per year of commitment - against which other national programs can be judged as serious or cosmetic.
insights.quote: Most recently, it committed SGD $37 billion ($29 billion in US dollars)—roughly 1% of GDP—over the next 5 years to driving research, innovation, and enterprise
insights.locator: Ingredient 4: Increasing Supportive Policy

insights.claim: Singapore's institutional design lesson is consolidation: Enterprise Singapore folded grants, equity financing, mentorship and global networking into one initiative, Startup SG, and its Global Innovation Alliance has connected more than 700 startups to partners in over 50 countries.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Single-agency consolidation, not headline funding size, is the differentiator worth checking when assessing rival national startup programs.
insights.quote: a single initiative, Startup SG, that enables founders to navigate public resources without bureaucratic friction
insights.locator: The government created Enterprise Singapore

insights.claim: Copenhagen moved from rank 71 to 48 largely through founder-built cultural infrastructure: TechBBQ, started in 2013 as an informal barbeque, now draws over 10,000 attendees as Scandinavia's largest startup conference.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The cheapest ingredient in the playbook is culture, and it is founder-initiated rather than state-funded - a low-cost intervention point for cities with thin budgets.
insights.quote: TechBBQ, launched in 2013 by a small group of Danish entrepreneurs, began as an informal gathering—a barbeque—designed to bring the city’s scattered startup community into one place.
insights.locator: Ingredient 5: Creating Community and Culture

insights.claim: Copenhagen's year-round ecosystem infrastructure includes Symbion, which supports around 550 startups and scaleups across five campuses, and Beyond Beta, Denmark's largest accelerator, which has helped more than 600 startups raise capital with participants growing headcount an average of 28% during the program.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Gives a hard accelerator performance metric (28% headcount growth during program) usable as a comparison baseline when evaluating other accelerator programs.
insights.quote: has helped more than 600 startups raise capital, with participating companies growing an average of 28% in head count during the program
insights.locator: That energy carries through the rest of the year

themes.theme: The measurement stack and its limits

insights.claim: The analysis rests entirely on StartupBlink's Global Startup Ecosystem Index, which ranks more than 1,400 city ecosystems across 118 countries and has published annually since 2017, with 'rapid risers' defined as cities gaining at least 20 places between the 2017 and 2025 editions.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Names the free, replicable dataset behind the conclusions - an investor can rerun the same rapid-riser screen independently rather than take BCG's 16-city list on trust.
insights.quote: This independent index uses quantitative data to evaluate and rank more than 1,400 city ecosystems across 118 countries over time.
insights.locator: How Did We Identify the Rapid Risers?

insights.claim: Because city ecosystem rankings have been relatively stable over the past decade, a jump in a city's ranking is treated as a reliable signal of trajectory rather than noise.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Rank stability is what makes the delta tradeable: monitor annual index movers as a low-frequency screen for cities whose local economies are inflecting.
insights.quote: These city rankings have proven to be relatively stable over the past decade, so jumps in a city’s ranking tend to be a reliable signal of that city’s trajectory.
insights.locator: The first ranking was published in 2017

insights.claim: Half of the 16 rapid risers started outside the top 150 in 2017 and all were outside the top 30, meaning the entire cohort's gains came from a very low base.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Tempers the read-across: 20-place gains are far easier from rank 150 than from rank 40, so the mid-tier ($700B) extrapolation may overstate achievable improvement.
insights.quote: In 2017, all the rapid risers were ranked outside of the top 30 cities in the Global Startup Ecosystem Index, and half were outside of the top 150.
insights.locator: In 2017, all the rapid risers were ranked
